passage: The school theatre club had a tradition: on show day everyone wore black and, before the curtain, mocked the rival drama group with a short parody. Trisha loved the club. Twelve people, one captain, Jomon, and the best hours of her week. This year she stood in the circle as the parody script was passed round. Everyone laughed. She stayed silent, then spoke. “I'll wear black and paint the sets, but I'd rather not do the parody.” Jomon raised an eyebrow. “It's tradition.” “I know. I still want to be here.” A boy shrugged. Two others nodded. Jomon paused, then said, “Fine. Sets and lights, then.” Trisha exhaled.

qa.q: How many people were in the theatre club?
qa.a: Twelve people were in the club.

qa.q: What did Trisha feel as she stood in the circle while everyone laughed at the parody script?
qa.a: Trisha felt uneasy and torn, since she loved the club but did not want to join the mockery.

qa.q: What choice did Trisha make that let her keep both her place and her view?
qa.a: Trisha offered to wear black and paint the sets but said she would rather not do the parody, and added that she still wanted to be there.

qa.q: How might Jomon have seen Trisha's refusal?
qa.a: Jomon probably felt challenged by a break in tradition but wanted to keep Trisha in the club, which fits the pause and the offer of sets and lights.

grounding: A teenager belongs to a group while holding a private view and steps back from one ritual with respect.

passage:
“Practice at six, boys,” Tanuja called across the community-centre yard, coach of the youth football group. “And before you ask, yes, we are still the best team in the colony.”
“Best,” chorused the others.
Mohit lingered at the back. “Tanuja didi, can I say something? I'm skipping Saturday film night. I'd rather go to my dance class.”
Someone snorted. “Dance?”
Tanuja looked around. “Anyone else have a problem with that?” Nobody spoke. “Mohit is on the team, and he's here at six every day. Film night is optional.”
Mohit let out a long breath. “Thanks.” A younger boy whispered, “Can you show me some moves?”

qa.q: Where does the football group practise at six?
qa.a: They practise in the community-centre yard.

qa.q: What was Mohit feeling when Mohit lingered at the back and asked, “can I say something?”
qa.a: Mohit was nervous about being teased but wanted to be honest about a different interest.

qa.q: What did Tanuja's response do for the group?
qa.a: Tanuja backed Mohit as a team member, said film night was optional and let the group see that belonging does not need sameness.

qa.q: What might the younger boy who asked for moves have been feeling?
qa.a: The younger boy may have felt curious and relieved that a different interest was accepted, and wanted to try it too.

grounding: A teenager belongs to a community while holding some private views, and the group shows that belonging does not need sameness.

passage: Last year I'd have quit the colony's Ganesh mandal. The older boys wanted a DJ blasting till midnight, and I hate that noise; our neighbour's baby cried every night. Everyone else said yes. I said no, out loud, in the meeting. It was awkward. Someone called me 'uncle'. But Ishita, who runs the decorations, said, 'Madhav's allowed to think that. Can he still help with the lights?' And I did. I stayed till two in the morning wiring the pandal, and I laughed with the same boys who'd teased me. I didn't change my mind about the DJ. They didn't change theirs. We ended up agreeing on ten o'clock. I'm still one of them, just a slightly quieter one.

qa.q: What did Madhav help with at the pandal?
qa.a: Wiring the lights, till two in the morning.

qa.q: How did Madhav feel after speaking against the DJ?
qa.a: He felt awkward and exposed, especially when teased, but still wanted to stay part of the mandal.

qa.q: What did Ishita do that helped the group allow difference?
qa.a: Ishita said Madhav was allowed his view and invited him to keep helping, showing that disagreeing didn't mean leaving.

qa.q: How might the older boys see Madhav by the end?
qa.a: They teased him at first, but after he worked till two and laughed with them, they likely saw him as still one of them, just with a different view.

grounding: A teenager keeps belonging to a community group while holding a different view, and the group makes room for it.

passage: Youth club leader's note, Sunday. Simran joined the football team in June and fitted in quickly. This week the team started a pre-match chant that mocks the other side's town. Simran didn't join in; she just clapped for our own players. A few teammates asked if she thought she was better than them. She said, 'No. I just cheer for us, not against them.' Rafiq, the captain, backed her: 'She's on the team. That's what matters.' I spoke to the team afterwards and said I was glad someone could belong here without copying everyone, and that good teams have room for that. Simran scored in the second half, and the whole bench mobbed her. Next week I will ask the team to write a new chant together.

qa.q: What did Simran say when asked if she thought she was better?
qa.a: 'No. I just cheer for us, not against them.'

qa.q: How might Simran have felt when teammates questioned her?
qa.a: She was probably uncomfortable and a little anxious about being seen as superior, yet steady enough to explain calmly.

qa.q: What did the leader do to help the team make room for difference?
qa.a: Told the team that belonging doesn't require copying everyone, and planned for them to write a new chant together.

qa.q: Why might Rafiq have backed Simran?
qa.a: As captain, Rafiq values the team over sameness, and may have seen that her way still supported the team.

grounding: A youth leader's note on a teenager who belongs to a team while quietly not joining a mocking chant.

passage:
Diary, Friday.
Our group decided the science fair is 'for nerds' and nobody's entering. Elizabeth said it first, and everyone nodded. I didn't say anything, but I'd already started my water-filter model, and honestly I love it.
Today I told them I'm entering anyway. Silence. Then Aditi said, 'So you're a nerd now?' I laughed and said, 'Always was. You just didn't notice.'
I was scared they'd drop me from lunch. They didn't. Elizabeth even asked how the filter works, and at the end she said, 'Okay, fine, we'll come and clap.'
I'm still in the group. I'm just the one with the filter.
Keerthana

qa.q: What model had Keerthana started?
qa.a: A water-filter model.

qa.q: What was Keerthana afraid of before telling the group?
qa.a: Keerthana was scared of being dropped from the lunch group for going against their decision.

qa.q: What in Keerthana's approach helped keep both the friendship and the choice?
qa.a: Saying it lightly with a joke, not attacking the group's view, and staying at lunch as usual.

qa.q: How did Elizabeth's view seem to shift?
qa.a: She started the 'for nerds' idea but then asked how the filter works and promised to come and clap, showing the group could hold a difference.

grounding: A teenager stays in a friend group while making a different choice, and the group turns out to allow it.
